But the argument reframes iterativity as a property of conversational dynamics: a proposition is in common ground when its negation or removal would trigger repair sequences (explicit challenges, clarifications) rather than silent update. The key premise is that this repair-theoretic criterion explains the same data about what can be felicitously presupposed, but without requiring any particular mental state configuration—it works equally well for pretense, strategic discourse, and ordinary belief-based conversation. The debate about mental state iteration is thus orthogonal to the phenomenon.
target: Both Stalnaker's and Yalcin's assumption that solving the iteration problem for mental states is what explains which propositions are in common ground
risk: This might merely push the question back: what determines when removal triggers repair might itself depend on mental states, making this a redescription rather than a reframing.
promise_reason: Repair-theoretic reframing of iterativity is clever and potentially unifying, though whether it genuinely bypasses mental states needs more development.

thesis: If common ground is defined by public commitments rather than mental states, then testimonial knowledge transmission fails, because a hearer can only acquire knowledge from testimony when the speaker's assertion manifests their belief, but public commitment accounts sever the constitutive link between assertion and belief.
sketch: Proponents of public-commitment theories of common ground argue they better handle cases where mental states diverge from conversational score. But testimonial knowledge (on most accounts) requires that assertion reliably indicates belief—I can learn that p from your telling me p only if your telling me p is grounded in your believing p. The key premise is that if assertion constitutively adds to public commitment scorekeeping rather than constitutively expressing belief, then assertion becomes unmoored from belief in a way that makes testimonial transmission mysterious. You'd need a separate story about why assertions track beliefs well enough for testimony to work, reintroducing the very mental-state constraints the public-commitment view was meant to avoid.
target: The position that common ground should be reconceived as public commitment scorekeeping independent of participants' mental states
risk: Public commitment theorists might accept this and offer a revisionary account of testimony, or argue that assertion has a dual nature (both expressing belief and creating commitment) rather than being purely one or the other.
promise_reason: Competent argument linking commitment theories to testimony, but the connection between assertion and belief is well-trodden territory and the incompatibility may not be as stark as claimed.

thesis: Acceptance in conversation is not an attitude toward propositions at all, but an undertaking of normative commitment to a proposition's dialectical availability, which explains why it tracks public action rather than private psychology.
sketch: Both Stalnaker and Yalcin treat acceptance as a distinctive mental attitude (whether voluntary or not, iterative or not). But the argument reframes acceptance as fundamentally a speech act or undertaking: to accept p conversationally is to make p available as a premise, assumption, or conversational anchor, thereby incurring obligations (to withdraw it explicitly if challenged, to maintain consistency with it, etc.). The key premise is that what matters for conversational dynamics is not what's in anyone's head but what commitments have been publicly undertaken. This is why you can 'accept' a proposition for conversation while believing it false (in legal contexts) or while knowing nobody believes it (in pretense). The attitude-talk is a misleading gloss on what is really a public, normative, action-theoretic phenomenon. Common ground is then the set of propositions all participants have undertaken to treat as available.
target: Both Stalnaker's and Yalcin's treatment of acceptance as a mental attitude rather than a normative status
risk: This may reduce to a terminological move if undertaking commitments still requires having certain mental states (intentions, decisions), making it unclear whether we've escaped mental-state dependency.
promise_reason: Reframes acceptance as normative undertaking rather than attitude; the move from mental to normative is familiar from broader speech act literature, limiting novelty.

thesis: Stalnaker's and Yalcin's accounts both collapse into forms of public commitment theory because their iteration conditions (whether for belief or knowledge) cannot be met without public evidence, making the mental states epiphenomenal to the public record.
sketch: The argument shows that both accounts require higher-order attitudes: Stalnaker needs mutual belief that mutual belief that... p, while Yalcin needs mutual knowledge that p is accepted. But the key premise is that such iteration is only achievable and verifiable through public manifestation — there's no way to get common knowledge or iterated belief 'off the ground' except through public acts (assertions, acknowledgments, shared experiences). Once we trace through how these iterations actually get established in conversation, we find they're always parasitic on a public record of who said what, what was acknowledged, what remains unchallenged. The mental states end up being either unverifiable posits or simply redescriptions of what the public record already determines. Both views therefore collapse into the claim that common ground is constituted by public commitments, with mental states as mere accompaniments.
target: Both Stalnaker's mental-state-based account and Yalcin's hybrid view
risk: The accounts might be defended by distinguishing epistemic grounds (public) from metaphysical constitution (mental), arguing that public evidence justifies ascription of mental states without making them epiphenomenal.
promise_reason: The collapse argument is interesting but the claim that mental states become epiphenomenal once we trace iteration conditions needs more work to be convincing.

thesis: The cases that pressure mental-state theories (pretense, bargaining, institutional speech) aren't exceptions but the norm: all conversational common ground is constituted by public commitment because even in 'sincere' conversation, coordination requires only mutual recognition of what's been put on record, not shared mental states.
sketch: Standard mental-state theories treat pretense and bargaining as special cases requiring separate explanation, while 'normal' conversation involves genuine shared belief or acceptance. But the argument reverses this: the key premise is that even in apparently sincere conversation, what enables coordination is not that we share mental states but that we mutually recognize what's been publicly established. When you assert p and I don't challenge it, p enters the common ground — not because we now share a belief or acceptance of p (I might be distracted, you might be lying), but because we both recognize that p is now on the public record as something that can be presupposed. The 'special' cases simply make obvious what's always true: common ground is a structure of mutually recognized public commitments. Mental states matter only insofar as they motivate making or tracking public commitments.
target: The dialectical framing that treats sincere conversation as basic and strategic/pretense cases as derivative exceptions
risk: This might be rejected as too deflationary if it can't explain why some conversational contexts feel like genuine sharing of minds rather than mere coordination on a public record.
promise_reason: Argues problematic cases reveal the norm rather than exceptions; the inversion is provocative but the argument that sincere conversation works the same way needs more support.

thesis: Acceptance comes in two fundamentally different kinds: psychological acceptance (an attitude) and positional acceptance (occupying a role in a normative structure), and Stalnaker/Yalcin equivocate between them, treating evidence about one as evidence about the other.
sketch: The distinction cuts between taking-to-be-true-for-reasoning-purposes (psychological) and being-on-record-as-committed-to (positional). The argument shows that these have different iteration properties: psychological acceptance might not iterate (Yalcin's point) while positional acceptance necessarily does—if I'm publicly committed to p and you're publicly committed to recognizing my commitment to p, then we're in the iterated state regardless of our psychological states. The equivocation explains why both Stalnaker and Yalcin find their respective packages natural: they're each tracking one kind while assuming they've characterized acceptance generally. Pretense, bargaining, and institutional discourse involve positional acceptance without psychological acceptance.
target: Both Stalnaker's and Yalcin's accounts of acceptance as a unified phenomenon
risk: Positional acceptance might reduce to a special case of psychological acceptance—perhaps acceptance of the proposition that one is committed to p—collapsing the distinction into a mere scope difference.
promise_reason: Distinguishing psychological from positional acceptance is useful but the equivocation charge needs more evidence that theorists actually conflate them rather than focusing on one.

thesis: Common ground is not a state at all but a transition system: it consists in the rules governing what updates are admissible given the history of the conversation, with no requirement that any state—mental or public—persist across updates.
sketch: The argument draws on dynamic semantics and process philosophy: just as a game is not a board-state but rules governing transitions between states, common ground is the system of constraints on what can come next. This explains accommodation (the rules themselves update), presupposition failure (certain moves become impermissible), and why pretense works (the transition rules apply regardless of beliefs). The key premise is that we mistake the common ground for snapshots of it (the propositions currently in play) when it's actually constituted by the operational rules. Mental states and public commitments are both inputs to the transition system, not the ground itself.
target: The assumption shared by both camps that common ground is a state (mental or otherwise) rather than a dynamic process
risk: The transition rules might themselves need to be mentally represented by participants to be operative, reducing the view to a complex version of the mental-state account, or the rules might just be abstractions from patterns in mental states.
promise_reason: Process-theoretic reconception is interesting but the claim that common ground is transition rules rather than states may be more terminological than substantive.

thesis: Treating common ground as mental commits you to the claim that conversational participants are massively mistaken about what they're doing: they systematically treat public commitment as authoritative over private attitude when the two come apart, but if common ground is mental, private attitude should be authoritative.
sketch: The argument identifies cases where speakers explicitly defer to the public record over their own memories and attitudes: 'I don't remember whether I accepted that, let's check the transcript'; 'You're committed to p by what you said, even if you've changed your mind'; legal proceedings where what's on the record trumps what the attorney believes. If common ground is mental, these practices are confused—participants should correct the record to match their attitudes. But competent participants recognize these situations as not confused at all; the public record has independent authority. Mentalists are thus committed to saying conversational participants are systematically confused about the structure of their own practice, which is a heavy theoretical cost. The key premise: participants' authoritative self-understanding of their practice counts against theories that make that understanding erroneous.
target: Both Stalnaker and Yalcin's mentalist assumptions
risk: The practices might be derivative: we defer to the public record precisely because it's better evidence of the mental states than our own current memory, making it epistemically but not metaphysically authoritative, which saves the mentalist account.
promise_reason: The argument from participants' self-understanding is methodologically interesting but the examples of deference to public record may have mental-state explanations available.

thesis: Conversational common ground is constituted by what participants are committed to treating as shared, not by any mental states of the participants, and this commitment relation is normative and irreducible—it cannot be analyzed in terms of beliefs, acceptances, or knowledge about commitments.
sketch: The argument starts from cases where discourse functions perfectly despite universal knowledge that no participant has the relevant mental state: legal fictions ('the corporation believes'), bargaining ('suppose we agree to $500'), and diplomatic language ('the Minister regrets'). The key premise is that these are not degenerate or parasitic cases but reveal what's fundamental: common ground is constituted by a normative structure of what participants may and must treat as shared in the conversation. Mental states like belief or acceptance typically track this structure, but they track it because the normative structure is prior, not because they constitute it. This dissolves the puzzles about pretense and strategic discourse: they're not cases where common ground comes apart from mental states, but cases where the mental state theory mistook effect for cause.
target: Both Stalnaker's and Yalcin's mentalism—the assumption that common ground must be defined as a configuration of participants' mental states
risk: The notion of 'normative commitment' may be too obscure to do explanatory work, or it might collapse back into mental states (commitments are just what we take ourselves to be bound by, which is a mental state about norms).
promise_reason: Argues for irreducible normative constitution with legal fictions as central cases; competent but the priority claim about normative structure needs more argument.

thesis: Any account that defines common ground in terms of propositional attitudes (belief, acceptance, knowledge) is committed to the impossibility of genuine presupposition failure, because presupposition requires that something NOT in common ground be treated as if it were, but attitude-based accounts make this description incoherent.
sketch: The argument targets the accommodation cases that both theorists discuss. When someone says 'my sister is visiting' and the hearer didn't know the speaker had a sister, we describe this as presupposition failure followed by accommodation. But if common ground just IS the relevant shared attitudes, then either the speaker was wrong about what was in common ground (it wasn't a genuine presupposition) or accommodation happened instantly and there was no failure. The key premise is that presupposition failure requires a gap between what the speaker treated as common ground and what actually was common ground, but on attitude-based accounts, there's no 'what actually was' independent of what participants take to be shared. This commits attitude theorists to either eliminativism about presupposition failure or to positing common ground as an independent entity that attitudes track—undermining the attitude-based account.
target: All attitude-based accounts of common ground, including both Stalnaker's and Yalcin's
risk: Theorists might bite the bullet and accept that 'presupposition failure' is just mutual false belief about what attitudes are shared, which is awkward but not obviously incoherent.
promise_reason: Points to tension about presupposition failure in attitude accounts but the incoherence charge may overstate the problem—theorists can distinguish actual from treated-as-shared.

thesis: Conversational common ground is the fiction that participants collectively maintain, where 'fiction' is primitive—this makes pretense, legal discourse, and ordinary assertion instances of the same fundamental phenomenon rather than the problematic periphery.
sketch: The argument inverts the usual explanatory priority. Instead of treating pretense and institutional discourse as special cases requiring explanation against a background of ordinary belief-driven conversation, we should recognize that all conversational common ground has the structure of collective fiction: participants jointly maintain a body of propositions 'in play' for purposes of the conversation, bracketing the question of their truth or anyone's actual attitudes toward them. Ordinary conversation is then the special case where the fiction happens to align with participants' beliefs. The key premise is that the core puzzles (pretense, bargaining, strategic discourse) aren't exceptions to be explained away but reveal the essential structure: common ground is what Lewis called 'make-believe' all the way down. This explains why public commitment matters and why mental states underdetermine conversational function.
target: The shared assumption that ordinary conversation is the explanatory base case and other forms of discourse are derivative or parasitic
risk: Calling everything 'fiction' may be merely relabeling the problem rather than solving it, and the account might struggle to explain why belief typically does align with what's in common ground if belief is genuinely peripheral.
promise_reason: Inverts explanatory priority to make fiction fundamental; provocative but 'fiction' as primitive needs more development and may just relabel the phenomenon.

thesis: Common ground is not a context-independent structure but a relation between a public commitment slate and a discourse purpose, such that the same public commitments constitute different common grounds when embedded in different activity types.
sketch: Both Stalnaker and Yalcin treat common ground as a determinate state (mental or hybrid) at a given moment, but this cannot explain why the same mutually known commitments function differently in bargaining versus testimony versus pretense. The argument turns on cases where parties bargaining over a house price have publicly committed to 'the house is worth $500K' but this functions as a negotiating anchor (neither believes it, both know this, it still structures the discourse), whereas the same commitment structure in testimony would constitute genuine common ground. The key premise: discourse purpose is not merely pragmatic overlay but metaphysically constitutive of what commitments amount to as common ground.
target: The shared assumption between Stalnaker and Yalcin that common ground has a context-independent metaphysical profile
risk: May collapse into the triviality that context matters, or fail to provide principled identity conditions for 'discourse purposes' that aren't just redescriptions of common ground differences
promise_reason: Competent observation that context matters, but the metaphysical claim about constitution is overstated and the bargaining example doesn't clearly establish the strong thesis.

thesis: Treating conversational common ground as jointly maintained public commitments (rather than mental states) commits you to rejecting the pretheoretic datum that participants can be mistaken about what the common ground is, which collapses the view into scorekeeping eliminativism.
sketch: If common ground is constituted by public commitments rather than participant mental states, then there is no gap between what commitments have actually been publicly undertaken and what the common ground is. But participants clearly can and do make mistakes about what has been mutually established—thinking something was agreed when it wasn't, or vice versa. The key premise: public commitment theorists must either deny these are genuine mistakes (making them eliminativists about the phenomenon) or smuggle mental states back in to create the gap between reality and appearance. Either horn is unstable: eliminativism abandons the explanatory target; smuggling maintains the view is really mentalist after all.
target: The move away from Stalnaker/Yalcin toward public commitment theories
risk: Public commitment theorists might accept a scorekeeper-relative notion of common ground, or argue that mistakes are about which commitments were publicly undertaken, not about common ground per se
promise_reason: Identifies a real tension but the dilemma is escapable—public commitment theorists have resources to distinguish constitutive commitments from participant tracking thereof.

thesis: Common ground is not a single phenomenon but two irreducibly different relations: interpersonal common ground (what we mutually know each other accepts) and discourse common ground (what commitments the conversation itself imposes on subsequent moves), which can come apart.
sketch: The argument proceeds by showing that the two relations have different persistence conditions and different defeasibility profiles. Interpersonal common ground is defeated when any participant's mental state changes or is revealed to be different than thought. Discourse common ground persists even through such revelations—when it becomes common knowledge that nobody believes p, p can still constrain what counts as a permissible conversational move (as in legal proceedings or formal negotiations). The key premise is that a single concept cannot have both sets of defeat conditions simultaneously. This explains why strategic discourse and pretense feel like genuine constraint despite transparent disbelief: they are constrained by discourse common ground even when interpersonal common ground is absent.
target: The shared assumption between Stalnaker and Yalcin that common ground is a unitary phenomenon tracking mental states
risk: The two alleged phenomena might be reducible to a single complex mental state structure involving acceptance-for-purposes-of-this-conversation, which is still mental but context-indexed
promise_reason: The two-relation view is plausible but splitting phenomena is a familiar move; the different defeat conditions are interesting but not sufficiently developed here.

thesis: Conversational common ground is the public commitments that would rationalize the speech acts that have already occurred, making it a backward-looking interpretive construct rather than a forward-looking constraint on rational speech.
sketch: Standard views treat common ground as what makes current speech acts felicitous or rational. But this gets the order of explanation backwards. The argument turns on this premise: speech acts themselves are the primary data, and common ground is whatever we must posit to make sense of them as rational moves. This is why presupposition accommodation works—not because hearers charitably add propositions to a pre-existing mental state, but because interpreters construct what common ground must have been to rationalize the speech act just performed. This explains discourse that proceeds 'as if' while everyone knows it's pretense: the speech acts occur, and common ground is whatever makes them interpretable as moves in that practice, regardless of participants' attitudes. The view makes common ground dependent on speech acts rather than vice versa.
target: Both Stalnaker and Yalcin's forward-looking, constraint-based conception of common ground
risk: This might collapse into a familiar coherentist or interpretivist view of meaning generally, losing what's distinctive about common ground as opposed to any other aspect of conversational interpretation
promise_reason: The backward-looking interpretive view is intriguing but not entirely new (echoes Davidson, Brandom); the accommodation explanation needs more work to be convincing.

thesis: Treating common ground as mental commits you to the claim that insincere testimony cannot generate common ground, but testimony characteristically does generate common ground even when the speaker's insincerity is itself common knowledge.
sketch: If common ground is constituted by participants' mental states (beliefs, acceptances, or knowledge thereof), then when a speaker's insincerity is transparent—everyone knows the testifier doesn't believe p—p cannot enter common ground, since the required mental states are absent. But in institutional contexts (courtroom testimony, official statements, diplomatic communications), insincere testimony routinely creates common ground: the proposition becomes what must be addressed, what subsequent speech acts must orient to, what can be presupposed. The key premise is that mental-state accounts make common ground supervene on psychological facts, and psychological facts include the speaker's actual attitudes. Therefore mental-state theorists must either deny that insincere-but-known testimony creates common ground (revisionist and implausible) or admit that common ground doesn't supervene on mental states after all (abandoning the mental view).
target: Both Stalnaker and Yalcin's assumption that context is a state of participants' minds
risk: Mental-state theorists might argue that acceptance or acceptance-for-conversational-purposes doesn't require sincerity, so transparent insincerity is compatible with the relevant mental states being present
promise_reason: The insincere testimony case is good but the argument has been made in various forms; institutional contexts doing this work is somewhat familiar territory.

thesis: Common ground is the set of propositions entailed by the constitutive rules of whatever conversational game is being played, making it prior to and independent of participants' mental states, which merely track or respond to those rules.
sketch: The argument begins from the observation that different conversational genres (bargaining, legal proceedings, storytelling, strategic discussion, collaborative inquiry) have different rules for what moves are permissible, what must be addressed, what can be presupposed. The key premise is that these rules constitute the game being played and are prior to any particular players' psychology—they're public, learnable, and remain stable across participants. What we call common ground in any conversation is just the propositions entailed by whichever game's rules are operative. Mental states (belief, acceptance, knowledge) are then effects rather than constituents: competent players form attitudes that align with the game's commitments, but the commitments don't depend on the attitudes. This explains why pretense and strategic discourse have genuine common ground structure despite absent belief: they're games with determinate rules, and common ground is rule-constituted, not mind-constituted.
target: The foundational assumption shared by Stalnaker and Yalcin that common ground is constituted by mental states
risk: This might be unable to explain how conversational games get selected or initiated except by appeal to participants' intentions and recognitions, smuggling mental states back in as foundational
promise_reason: The game-theoretic constitutive rules approach is well-developed elsewhere; applying it to common ground is natural but not groundbreaking.

thesis: Acceptance is not a uniform phenomenon but fractures into at least three functional kinds—coordinative acceptance (for joint action), dialectical acceptance (for argument structure), and stipulative acceptance (for contextual framing)—and common ground is actually a heterogeneous bundle of these tracked separately, which is why it appears to come apart from both belief and voluntary commitment.
sketch: The argument begins with cases where these come apart: in legal discourse, lawyers coordinatively accept a stipulation (treating it as binding for their joint activity), dialectically accept an opponent's premise for reductio (treating it as in-play for argument), but stipulatively accept courtroom procedures (treating them as frame-setting). Each supports different presuppositions and licenses different accommodations. The key premise is that what Stalnaker and Yalcin both call 'acceptance' is a mongrel category, and the puzzles about pretense, bargaining, etc., arise because different components of this bundle can be present or absent independently. Common ground isn't one thing with mysterious properties, but several things philosophers have been wrong to unify.
target: Both Stalnaker's and Yalcin's assumption that acceptance is a single phenomenon that can be given one correct analysis
risk: The functional distinctions might not cut at the joints—perhaps all three are just contextual variations of a single underlying cognitive/social stance, making this over-classification rather than genuine heterogeneity.
promise_reason: Fracturing acceptance into types is reasonable but the heterogeneity diagnosis feels more like redescription than explanation of the puzzles.

thesis: Yalcin's position is unstable because common knowledge that p is accepted cannot explain accommodation—when accommodation occurs, participants do not first achieve common knowledge of mutual acceptance and then update common ground, but rather the very act of non-challenge constitutes acceptance, which means acceptance cannot be both voluntary and prior to common ground as Yalcin requires.
sketch: The argument targets Yalcin's claim that acceptance is voluntary but common ground requires common knowledge of acceptance. In standard accommodation cases (Lewis, von Fintel), a speaker presupposes p, hearers don't challenge, and p becomes common ground. But there's no moment where hearers voluntarily accept p and this becomes common knowledge before accommodation happens. The key premise is that accommodation is constitutive: the absence of challenge just is what makes p accepted/common ground, rather than being evidence of a prior voluntary acceptance. This means either acceptance isn't voluntary (it's constituted by non-challenge), or it isn't prior to common ground (common ground doesn't require common knowledge of acceptance), or accommodation is impossible. Since accommodation clearly happens, Yalcin must give up either the voluntariness or the priority claim.
target: Yalcin's position that acceptance is voluntary while common ground requires common knowledge of acceptance
risk: Yalcin might bite the bullet and say accommodation involves a very fast, often unconscious, voluntary acceptance that becomes common knowledge through the absence of challenge—the voluntariness is there, just not always phenomenologically salient.
promise_reason: Targets Yalcin specifically with a real tension about accommodation, but the instability argument needs more development to be fully convincing.

thesis: Holding that common ground is a mental state commits you to the possibility of true but unknowable presupposition failures—cases where discourse pragmatically fails despite all participants believing it's proceeding smoothly—which proponents of mental-state views must reject because it makes presupposition failure epistemically inaccessible in principle.
sketch: If common ground consists in iterated acceptance or common knowledge of acceptance (mental states), then whether p is common ground is a fact about participants' minds. But participants can be systematically wrong about their own higher-order mental states: I can believe that you believe that I believe p when in fact you don't, and you can have the symmetric error. The key premise is that such symmetric higher-order errors are possible (they occur in actual cases of mutual misunderstanding that only becomes apparent much later). This means there can be presupposition failures that no participant could possibly detect at the time—the discourse fails by the mental-state theorist's own lights, but everyone reasonably believes it's succeeding. Mental-state theorists must either accept this radical skepticism about presupposition or admit that common ground cannot be purely mental.
target: Mental-state theories of common ground (Stalnaker, Yalcin)
risk: Mental-state theorists might embrace this as a feature rather than bug—of course there can be unknowable presupposition failures, just as there can be unknowable false beliefs; this is just fallibilism about common ground, not a reductio.
promise_reason: The unknowable failure problem is philosophically interesting but the skeptical conclusion may be acceptable to mentalists; needs stronger dialectical pressure.

thesis: Acceptance cannot play the role Stalnaker and Yalcin assign it because acceptance is necessarily indexed to a practical context, yet common ground must be portable across contexts—and this portability requirement entails that common ground is constituted by public commitments rather than mental states.
sketch: When you accept p for conversational purposes, what you accept is 'p for the purposes of this conversation.' But conversational common ground must support deferred commitments: what we agree on now constrains what I can assert tomorrow, what you can presuppose next week, what third parties can attribute to our conversation. The key premise is that mental states like acceptance are essentially occasion-bound—my accepting p now, for these purposes, gives out when the purposes change—while the normative force of common ground persists. If I try to build persistence into acceptance ('accepting p across all future relevant contexts'), I've either made acceptance equivalent to belief (losing Yalcin's voluntariness), or I've smuggled in an appeal to public commitment (something like 'accepting that I'm on record about p'). Either way, acceptance-based accounts collapse: into belief-based accounts or into commitment-based accounts.
target: Both Stalnaker and Yalcin's use of acceptance (whether default or voluntary) as the mental state constituent of common ground
risk: One could argue that acceptance is portable precisely because it creates a standing intention to treat p as true in future contexts, and intentions are mental states that persist without needing public commitments.
promise_reason: The portability requirement is interesting and the context-indexing problem is real, but the collapse argument needs tightening to be fully effective.

thesis: If common ground is constituted by shared mental states, then participants who discover they never shared the mental state should be able to retract everything that depended on the supposed common ground—but retraction fails precisely in cases (testimony, contract) where common ground does most explanatory work, showing that common ground creates irreversible public commitments independent of mental states.
sketch: Suppose I testify to you that p, and you accept it, putting p in common ground. Later, you discover I never believed p (I was lying) or you discover you never really accepted it (you were being polite). On mental-state accounts, this discovery should mean p was never really in common ground, and you should be able to void all downstream commitments that relied on p—like discovering a contract clause you both misread. But the key premise is that in testimonial contexts, you remain committed: you've vouched for p to others, relied on it in action, testified in turn based on it. The mental-state failure doesn't void the common ground; instead, it creates entitlement to complaint ('you put me in a position where I committed to p'). This asymmetry—that entering common ground is constituted by mental states but being in common ground isn't—is unstable. The better explanation is that the testimonial exchange itself created public commitments that persist independent of whether the mental states obtained.
target: The assumption shared by mental-state theorists that common ground inherits its metaphysical structure from the mental states that constitute it
risk: One might argue this just shows common ground has normative consequences (downstream commitments) without showing it isn't constituted by mental states—mental states can create binding commitments that outlast them, like how signing a contract creates obligations independent of whether you still intend to comply.
promise_reason: The non-retractability point is interesting but the argument's force depends on contested claims about what mental-state theories predict.

thesis: Acceptance is not voluntary at the level relevant for common ground: conversational participants can be involuntarily committed to accepting propositions through accommodation mechanisms that bypass individual control.
sketch: Yalcin's argument that acceptance is voluntary depends on contrasting it with knowledge. But accommodation shows acceptance can be forced: when a speaker presupposes p and hearers don't immediately object, they become committed to accepting p for conversational purposes even if they neither chose to accept it nor noticed it was introduced. The key premise is that accommodation operates automatically and pre-reflectively—by the time you could voluntarily reject the acceptance, conversational damage is done and repair is needed. Examples include manipulative presuppositions ('Have you stopped cheating?') and rapid-fire discourse where presuppositions slip in. This shows acceptance has the same involuntary character Yalcin attributes to knowledge, undermining his primary distinction between them.
target: Yalcin's claim that acceptance is voluntary while knowledge is not
risk: Might conflate being committed to acceptance (by conversational dynamics) with actually accepting—the involuntariness might be at the wrong level
promise_reason: Undermines Yalcin's voluntarism about acceptance through accommodation, but the dialectical payoff is narrower than broader reframings.

thesis: Stalnaker's iterated acceptance account is unstable: once we allow acceptance without belief, the iteration clauses do no work, and common ground collapses into mere mutual public commitment without the mental-state層.
sketch: Stalnaker needs acceptance to be a mental state weaker than belief to handle non-doxastic cases, but he also needs the iteration (everyone accepts that everyone accepts that...) to do explanatory work. The key premise is that iteration only adds explanatory value when the iterated state has psychological reality—when it's belief or knowledge, higher orders matter for coordination. But if acceptance is just 'treating as true for conversational purposes,' then 'I accept that you accept p' adds nothing to 'we've both publicly committed to p.' The psychological reality that makes iteration interesting is precisely what acceptance-without-belief lacks. So Stalnaker must either restore belief as the primary notion (losing non-doxastic cases) or admit common ground is just public commitment structure (losing the mental-state analysis).
target: Stalnaker's attempt to maintain both mental-state analysis and coverage of non-doxastic discourse
risk: Might underestimate the psychological reality of non-doxastic acceptance states—perhaps there really is a difference between first-order and higher-order acceptance
promise_reason: Shows instability in Stalnaker's iteration when acceptance is weakened, but the dilemma may have responses not fully anticipated here.

thesis: Anyone who accepts that common ground explains presupposition accommodation is committed to common ground being a public structure rather than a mental state, because accommodation regularly occurs before participants form any corresponding mental states.
sketch: Presupposition accommodation is widely taken as a central datum that theories of common ground must explain. The key premise is that accommodation demonstrably happens faster than the formation of iterated mental states: a speaker presupposes p, and before hearers consciously register p, let alone form acceptances or mutual knowledge about p, they're already processing subsequent utterances that build on p. This is shown by garden-path presuppositions where hearers only consciously notice what they accommodated when later asked. If accommodation is immediate but mental states require processing time, then accommodation cannot be explained by mental-state common ground—it must be explained by immediate updates to a public structure. Therefore, theorists committed to common ground explaining accommodation are committed to public-structure accounts.
target: Mental-state theorists (both Stalnaker and Yalcin) who take presupposition accommodation as a core explanandum
risk: Mental-state theorists might accept unconscious or automatic mental states that form as quickly as public structure updates, blocking the timing argument
promise_reason: The timing argument about accommodation is empirically interesting but depends on processing claims that may be contested or refined.

thesis: Stalnaker's and Yalcin's frameworks both fail because they presuppose common ground must be a single uniform phenomenon, when in fact 'common ground' is a family resemblance concept covering distinct phenomena with different metaphysical profiles in cooperative discourse, strategic discourse, and institutional discourse.
sketch: The argument shows that the cases cited as counterexamples to mental state views (pretense, bargaining, legal speech) are not exceptions to be accommodated but evidence that 'common ground' names different things in different contexts. In cooperative inquiry, common ground is genuinely mental (mutual belief or acceptance). In strategic discourse, it is a public scorekeeping device tracking what moves are available, independent of attitudes. In institutional contexts, it is constituted by conventional stipulation. The pressure to find a unified account creates a false dilemma. The key premise is that the functional role of 'what is in play' varies so dramatically across discourse types that no single metaphysical account can capture all cases without distortion.
target: Both Stalnaker and Yalcin, insofar as they seek a unified account of common ground across discourse types
risk: This may dissolve a genuine phenomenon rather than explain it—the fact that all these contexts use the same presuppositional mechanisms and exhibit the same accommodation patterns suggests underlying unity, not mere family resemblance.
promise_reason: Family resemblance dissolution is methodologically interesting but risks being seen as giving up on the theoretical project rather than advancing it.

thesis: Public commitment theories of common ground are unstable: they collapse into mental state theories because a commitment can only constrain discourse if participants mentally represent it as constraining, which reintroduces acceptance or belief in the commitment itself as the real ground.
sketch: The argument targets the move away from mental states toward public commitments by showing it is incomplete. For a public commitment to do the work required of common ground—to make certain moves appropriate and others inappropriate—participants must be responsive to it. But responsiveness requires mental representation: I must believe/accept that commitment C is in place, and believe/accept that you believe/accept this. In pretense, we are all committed to acting as if p, but this only explains discourse proceeding as though p is in play if we accept that we are so committed. The key premise is that normative constraints on discourse are only efficacious through agents' mental states, so public commitment can at best be derivative on or parasitic upon a mental state common ground.
target: Theorists who argue common ground should be understood as public commitment rather than mental state
risk: This may conflate the grounds of a commitment with the grounds of its efficacy—public commitments might be metaphysically prior even if their causal operation requires mental representation, just as laws constrain behavior even though their efficacy requires agents who grasp them.
promise_reason: The regress argument that commitments require mental representation is clever but public-commitment theorists have responses about implicit vs explicit representation.

thesis: Treating common ground as what participants accept commits you to treating presupposition failure not as a cognitive mistake but as a moral breach, because acceptance is under voluntary control and thus subject to obligation.
sketch: If common ground is defined by acceptance rather than belief (as both Stalnaker and Yalcin agree), and acceptance is voluntary (as Yalcin explicitly argues), then failing to accept what is presupposed is not an epistemic error but a violation of conversational obligation—a refusal to go along with what one could choose to accept. This makes presupposition failure more like defection in a cooperative enterprise than like false belief. The key premise is that the voluntary/involuntary distinction tracks the moral/cognitive distinction: we are blameworthy for voluntary states in a way we are not for involuntary ones. This predicts that presupposition failure should feel like bad faith, not like confusion, and that accommodating failed presuppositions should feel like granting a request, not correcting an error.
target: Yalcin's characterization of acceptance as voluntary and his redefinition of common ground in terms of acceptance
risk: The voluntary/involuntary distinction may not track the moral/cognitive distinction cleanly—intentions are voluntary but can still be mistaken rather than blameworthy, and the phenomenology of presupposition failure often does involve confusion rather than perceived bad faith.
promise_reason: Connects voluntariness to moral vs cognitive failure in an original way, but the predicted phenomenology may not clearly favor this interpretation.

thesis: Common ground is a collective intentional state irreducible to the mental states of individual participants: it is the content of a we-intention to treat p as shared background, which explains how discourse can proceed as though p is in play even when no individual accepts p.
sketch: This reframes the debate by rejecting its individualist framing. Both mental state theories (which aggregate individual acceptances/beliefs) and public commitment theories (which avoid mentalism by going non-mental) miss that common ground is a genuinely collective mental state. In strategic or institutional discourse, we jointly intend to treat p as background without any individual accepting p, analogous to how an orchestra collectively intends to perform a symphony without any individual musician intending to perform the whole. The key premise is that collective intentionality is metaphysically primitive (following Searle, Bratman, or Gilbert) and cannot be reduced to individual mental states plus anything else. This explains pretense and institutional cases: we share an intention to proceed as though p, which is a mental state but not anyone's individual mental state.
target: The shared assumption that common ground must be either reducible to individual mental states or non-mental
risk: Collective intentionality may inherit all the problems of individual mental state theories if the we-intention still requires that participants accept or believe that *we* are treating p as background, pushing the problem back one level without solving it.
promise_reason: Collective intentionality is a legitimate alternative but depends on accepting primitiveness claims that remain controversial in social ontology.

thesis: Acceptance is neither voluntary nor iterative but artifactual: it is constituted by the existence of publicly accessible records (utterances, gestures, written marks) that license certain inferences about what is 'given' for purposes of the conversation.
sketch: The argument targets both Stalnaker and Yalcin by denying that acceptance is a mental act at all. Instead, 'acceptance' is a theoretical posit we use to explain the normative force of conversational artifacts. When someone says 'it's raining' and this is not challenged, the utterance itself becomes part of the conversational record, and participants orient to that record. The key premise is that all the work done by 'acceptance' can be done by the public accessibility and persistence of conversational artifacts plus norms about when challenges are required. This explains legal and institutional discourse perfectly: the court record determines what is 'accepted' regardless of anyone's mental state. It also explains why acceptance seems both voluntary (you can refuse to produce the artifact) and iterative (artifacts can be about artifacts) without being a mental state at all.
target: Both Stalnaker's and Yalcin's assumption that acceptance is a mental state or act, differing only on its properties
risk: Struggles to explain thought experiments involving purely mental conversation or cases where people converse without language, suggesting some notion of acceptance as mental may be ineliminable
promise_reason: Artifactual account is genuinely novel and handles institutional cases well, though it may struggle with purely verbal exchanges without records.

thesis: Common knowledge that p is accepted collapses into mere common knowledge that p, making Yalcin's redefinition extensionally equivalent to a standard epistemic account he intends to reject.
sketch: Yalcin moves from acceptance to 'common knowledge that p is accepted' to avoid voluntarism about knowledge. But if everyone commonly knows that p is accepted in the conversation, and acceptance's functional role is to treat p as a basis for reasoning, then common knowledge that p is accepted makes p commonly known to be a shared basis for reasoning—which is precisely what common knowledge that p accomplishes. The key instability premise: once acceptance is common knowledge, it does all the conversational work that the accepted content's truth would do if it were commonly known. The added layer of 'acceptance' becomes idle. In any context where acceptance matters (where it's used as a premise), common knowledge of acceptance delivers exactly what common knowledge of truth delivers. Yalcin's view thus collapses back into the simpler epistemic account where common ground is just common knowledge.
target: Yalcin's (2024) redefinition of common ground as common knowledge that p is accepted
risk: Yalcin might successfully argue that acceptance has distinct norms from belief (e.g., acceptance can be context-relative or temporary in ways belief cannot), so the two knowledge states genuinely differ
promise_reason: The collapse argument against Yalcin is direct but he may have resources to maintain the distinction between knowledge-of-acceptance and knowledge-of-truth.

thesis: If common ground is defined by acceptance and acceptance can be insincere (as in bargaining or legal contexts), then commitment to any acceptance-based theory of common ground entails commitment to the coherence of insincere presupposition, which even acceptance theorists reject.
sketch: Both Stalnaker and Yalcin define common ground partly in terms of acceptance, and both acknowledge acceptance can occur without belief. But if acceptance can be strategic or insincere (I accept p for the sake of argument while believing not-p), then common ground can contain insincerely accepted propositions. The key premise is that presupposition is standardly analyzed as requiring common ground membership. This generates a commitment: acceptance theorists must allow that one can insincerely presuppose—use a presupposition trigger for content one does not even accept in the conversational sense, but only seems to accept. Yet this seems incoherent: the presupposition failure when someone says 'the king of France is bald' is not fixed by their insincerely accepting there is a king of France. The acceptance theorist seems committed to distinguishing genuine from merely apparent acceptance, which reintroduces the mental-state requirements they wanted to liberalize.
target: Acceptance-based theories of common ground (both Stalnaker's and Yalcin's versions)
risk: Acceptance theorists might bite the bullet and accept insincere presupposition as coherent, or distinguish acceptance-in-the-conversation from acceptance-for-other-purposes in a principled way
promise_reason: Competent internal critique of acceptance theories, but the move from strategic acceptance to 'insincere presupposition' may equivocate on what acceptance theorists mean by acceptance in conversational contexts.

thesis: Acceptance comes in two fundamentally different kinds—role-acceptance (accepting-as) and content-acceptance (accepting-that)—and only the former is constitutive of common ground, which is why institutional and pretense contexts function normally without anyone accepting-that the content.
sketch: The argument draws a distinction both Stalnaker and Yalcin miss: when I accept p in a game of make-believe, I accept p *as a premise for this conversation*, not accept *that* p is true. Role-acceptance is relational (acceptance-for-purpose-X) while content-acceptance is absolute. This explains the puzzle cases: in legal discourse, everyone accepts 'the corporation is a person' as-a-legal-premise without accepting-that corporations are persons. Common ground is constituted by what participants role-accept for conversational purposes, which is why it can diverge completely from belief, knowledge, or even public commitment in the sense of what one would defend outside the conversation. The key premise is that acceptance has an often-suppressed argument place for the role or frame within which the acceptance operates.
target: Both Stalnaker's and Yalcin's undifferentiated notion of acceptance as a single attitude
risk: The distinction might be doing the same work as existing notions like 'acceptance in a context' or 'pretense', just with new terminology, or role-acceptance might itself require some mental state as its ground
promise_reason: The accepting-as/accepting-that distinction is useful and may have been undertheorized, but similar role-relative notions have been explored in the literature on acceptance.

thesis: Public commitment accounts are unstable because public commitments either require mental state backing (making them covertly mentalist) or float free as mere conversational scores (making presupposition accommodation inexplicable).
sketch: The argument targets public commitment views by showing they face a dilemma. Either public commitments must be grounded in participants' intentions to be bound (in which case we're back to mental states as constitutive), or they're just abstract scorekeeping with no connection to what participants must do. If the latter, it's mysterious why accommodation—updating common ground in response to presupposition—feels mandatory rather than optional. We can't just refuse to accommodate the way we can refuse to accept a conversational score in a game. But if commitments require mental backing, then cases where everyone knows nobody accepts the content show that the real work is being done by something other than commitment—perhaps by the appearance or pretense of commitment. The key premise is that normative force requires grounding in agent-involving states, but public commitments were supposed to avoid such grounding.
target: Public commitment accounts that try to avoid mental states
risk: There might be a stable middle position where commitments are constituted by public acts without requiring backing mental states, similar to how promising works on some views
promise_reason: The dilemma is clearly stated, but public commitment theorists have resources to resist both horns (e.g., constitutive rules that generate obligations without mental backing); the accommodation puzzle may not be decisive.

thesis: Conversational common ground is constituted by mutually recognized default presumptions rather than by any form of acceptance or commitment, which is why common ground persists through explicit denial and why adding to common ground doesn't require any uptake.
sketch: The argument reframes common ground as a default structure rather than a commitment structure. What makes p part of common ground is that p is what we're entitled to presume unless someone objects, and we mutually recognize this entitlement. This differs from acceptance (which is a pro-attitude) and commitment (which binds). It explains the puzzles: in pretense, we presume the pretense-content by default for conversational purposes even though nobody accepts it; in strategic discourse, we presume claims are true-for-discussion without committing to them. Crucially, this explains unilateral accommodation: speakers can add to common ground without uptake because they're establishing new defaults, and hearers who don't object are acquiescing to the presumption. The key premise is that defaults have different logic than acceptances—they require justification to remove rather than justification to add.
target: The shared assumption that common ground involves positive uptake (acceptance, commitment, or knowledge) rather than default presumption
risk: Presumptions might themselves be a kind of acceptance or commitment, or the account might not explain why some presumptions are more revisable than others
promise_reason: The default-presumption framework is interesting and may handle some cases well, but it's not clear this is more than terminological repackaging of existing positions about defeasible commitments.

thesis: Accepting p into common ground commits speakers to treating counterfactual variants of the conversation where p is false as defective, even when no participant believes or knows that p—this scorekeeping commitment, not psychological acceptance, explains presupposition projection.
sketch: The argument identifies an unnoticed normative commitment in the practice of acceptance. When parties accept p (even in pretense or negotiation), they thereby undertake to treat hypothetical continuations where p is denied as requiring special repair moves—challenges like 'but we agreed that...' or 'you're changing the rules.' This commitment holds even when everyone knows p is false (as in shared fiction) because it governs conversational score, not belief. The key premise is that presupposition projection patterns track these counterfactual scorekeeping commitments rather than actual psychological states. This shows that both Stalnaker and Yalcin miss what acceptance actually does: it creates normative structure over possible continuations, not mental states in participants.
target: Both Stalnaker's and Yalcin's accounts of what acceptance contributes to common ground
risk: The normative commitments might themselves reduce to complex higher-order beliefs about what participants are entitled to assume, returning us to mental states.
promise_reason: The counterfactual scorekeeping commitment is an interesting normative structure, but it's unclear whether this explains projection better than existing accounts or simply redescribes what needs explaining.

thesis: Stalnaker's iterative acceptance structure generates common ground that is too fragile (destroyed by one participant's private doubt), while Yalcin's common knowledge of acceptance generates common ground that is too robust (surviving public explicit rejection)—both failures stem from treating common ground as having determinate membership conditions rather than being essentially contested and negotiable.
sketch: The argument presents paired counterexamples. Against Stalnaker: in plea bargaining, both parties maintain common ground that the defendant is guilty even when the defense attorney privately doubts this—the iterated acceptance condition fails but the conversational common ground persists. Against Yalcin: in heated disagreement, a participant explicitly rejects a previously accepted premise ('I never accepted that!') yet the conversation continues to presuppose it and the rejecting party must actively work to dislodge it—common knowledge of acceptance is destroyed but common ground persists. The key premise is that common ground has vague boundaries and can be contested mid-conversation, which neither determinate membership condition can capture. This suggests common ground is not a precisely defined set but a negotiated territory with fuzzy borders.
target: Both Stalnaker's and Yalcin's attempts to give necessary and sufficient conditions for common ground membership
risk: The examples may show only that common ground can be mistaken about or that there are multiple kinds of common ground, rather than that it lacks determinate conditions.
promise_reason: The paired counterexamples are useful and the vagueness/negotiability point is worth developing, but the conclusion that common ground lacks determinate membership may be too quick.

thesis: The phenomenon theorists call 'accommodation' is actually exploitation of a standing ambiguity about whether common ground is descriptive (what is mutually believed/accepted) or prescriptive (what should be treated as settled for conversational purposes)—presupposition projects the prescriptive frame onto the descriptive reality, and this projection, not any psychological update, is what accommodation consists in.
sketch: This reframes the accommodation debate by arguing that common ground is Janus-faced: it simultaneously describes a social-epistemic state and prescribes conversational norms. When a speaker presupposes p, they assert prescriptive common ground status for p ('treat this as settled'), which may or may not match the descriptive common ground (what participants actually accept). Accommodation occurs when hearers choose to align descriptive with prescriptive rather than challenge the mismatch. The key premise is that this explains why accommodation feels optional yet often obligatory: hearers face a choice between two legitimate interpretations of what 'common ground' demands. This dissolves puzzles about how new information can enter common ground 'automatically'—it doesn't; rather, prescriptive framing licenses post-hoc descriptive alignment.
target: Standard theories of presupposition accommodation as automatic update of common ground
risk: The prescriptive/descriptive distinction may collapse if prescriptions about common ground are themselves part of common ground, creating circularity rather than explaining accommodation.
promise_reason: The descriptive/prescriptive ambiguity is interesting and may illuminate accommodation, but it's not clear this dissolves the puzzle rather than relabeling it (what grounds the prescriptive authority?).

thesis: Common ground is not the participants' shared mental state but rather the set of propositions that the participants are committed to treating as retractable only at defined procedural cost.
sketch: The argument proceeds by observing that in legal depositions, parliamentary debate, and contract negotiation, propositions enter and exit 'common ground' through explicit procedural moves (motions, stipulations, formal retractions) rather than through any change in participants' beliefs or acceptances. The key premise is that what matters for conversational dynamics is not what attitudes participants have toward p, but what *price* they would pay for acting as though not-p—where price can be social, procedural, or legal rather than epistemic. This explains why a proposition can remain 'in play' even when all parties know none of them believe it: retracting it would cost something (losing face, violating protocol, breaching contract), and that cost structure, not the mental states, is what conversation tracks.
target: The shared assumption between Stalnaker and Yalcin that common ground supervenes on participants' mental states (whether beliefs, acceptances, or knowledge thereof)
risk: May collapse into mere terminological revision if it turns out that 'commitment' is just another mental state, or if the procedural costs themselves ultimately reduce to expectations about others' mental states
promise_reason: The procedural-cost framework captures something important about institutional discourse, but may just be a variant of public commitment views rather than a genuine alternative.

thesis: The phenomenon of 'going on record' shows that common ground has a temporal structure (propositions are timestamped and immutable once entered) that no mental state account can capture, since mental states are continuously revisable.
sketch: In institutional contexts, it matters not just what is in common ground but when it entered: a claim made 'for the record' at time t cannot be altered by later mental state changes, only by procedural moves that acknowledge the earlier entry. The key distinction is between mutable mental states (which change when participants change their minds) and immutable public record (which preserves what was committed to when, even if everyone later wishes it weren't so). Mental state accounts cannot draw this distinction because mental states don't have the right temporal structure—if everyone ceases to accept p at t+1, then on mental state views p is no longer in common ground, but in many contexts p demonstrably remains in common ground pending formal retraction. This shows common ground must be at least partly constituted by something with archival persistence.
target: The shared assumption that common ground supervenes solely on participants' current mental states
risk: Mental state theorists might accommodate temporal structure through memories or meta-beliefs about what was previously accepted, making the distinction between mental and public record less sharp than claimed
promise_reason: The temporal immutability point is genuinely challenging for mental state views and the archival-persistence requirement is worth developing, though it may apply only to institutional contexts.

thesis: Presupposition accommodation proves that common ground cannot be a mental state, because accommodation adds propositions to common ground before any participant forms the relevant mental state, making mental states effects rather than constituents of common ground.
sketch: When a speaker presupposes p and hearers accommodate, the standard story is that p enters common ground. But the temporal order is: speaker acts as if p is common ground → hearers recognize this and update their mental states → p becomes common ground. The key premise is that the speaker's initial presupposing move is what does the work—it creates the common ground entry, and hearers' mental states update to match it, not the reverse. This means common ground is whatever the presupposing move operates on, and that cannot be mental states because those come later. Instead, presupposing is a public move that alters the conversational score directly, with mental states tracking the score rather than constituting it. This inverts the standard picture: instead of conversation tracking shared mental states, mental states track conversational score.
target: Both Stalnaker and Yalcin, who treat mental states as constitutive of common ground with conversation tracking them
risk: Opponents might argue that accommodation is near-instantaneous mental state updating, or that the speaker's presupposing is itself grounded in their mental state, preserving the mental-state-first picture
promise_reason: The temporal-order argument about accommodation is interesting but mental state theorists can reply that accommodation involves rapid mental state formation, or that the speaker's presupposition is itself a mental state that triggers coordination.

thesis: Yalcin's position that common knowledge of acceptance can replace iterated acceptance is unstable because knowing that someone accepts p without iterating one's own acceptance makes their acceptance strategically manipulable information rather than common ground, collapsing his view back toward public commitment accounts.
sketch: If I know you accept p but I don't accept p myself, your acceptance becomes a fact I can strategically use—I can exploit it, manipulate it, or bargain with it. This is precisely what happens in strategic discourse. The key premise is that genuine common ground must constrain all participants equally and cannot create asymmetries of strategic advantage. But Yalcin's common knowledge of acceptance allows precisely such asymmetries: you're committed by your acceptance, I know this, but I'm not similarly committed. This asymmetry means it functions like public commitment (which explicitly allows agents to track what others are committed to without being committed themselves) rather than like a shared mental context. The instability is that trying to make common ground less mentalistic by dropping iteration actually pushes it toward the public commitment view Yalcin presumably wanted to avoid.
target: Yalcin's proposal to replace iterated acceptance with common knowledge of acceptance
risk: Yalcin might accept this consequence and embrace a public commitment account, or argue that the asymmetry is a feature not a bug for explaining strategic discourse
promise_reason: Competent internal critique of Yalcin showing instability, but the strategic manipulability point has been made in adjacent literatures.

thesis: The debate between mental-state and public-commitment accounts of common ground is partially verbal: both sides are tracking different phenomena that ordinary language conflates under 'common ground'—mutual belief versus dialectical common ground—and fiction reveals they can come apart because fictional discourse requires dialectical common ground (coordinated uptake of the pretense) but prohibits mutual belief in the content.
sketch: When we engage with fiction, we need something like common ground to coordinate our interpretations and build on each other's contributions ('Yes, and Holmes then deduced...'), but this cannot be mutual belief since we all know Holmes doesn't exist. The key premise is that the coordinating function attributed to common ground is actually served by dialectical common ground (mutual readiness to proceed as if p for discourse purposes), while the rationalizing function (explaining why speakers choose utterances) is served by mutual belief about what others believe. Fiction works precisely because dialectical common ground can operate without mutual belief. The debate appears substantive because both theorists assume one phenomenon, but they're emphasizing different functions. Stalnaker emphasizes the rationalizing function (why speakers choose their words), which does require beliefs; public commitment theorists emphasize the coordinating function (how discourse proceeds), which only requires tracking public commitments.
target: The framing that treats mental-state and public-commitment views as competing accounts of a single phenomenon
risk: One side might successfully argue that one of these functions is clearly the primary or definitional role of common ground, making the other derivative rather than equally fundamental
promise_reason: Deflationary 'both are right' moves are common; fiction case is nice but unlikely to convince either side they're tracking different phenomena.

thesis: Common ground is not a single phenomenon but two distinct mechanisms—conversational score (public commitments) and shared suppositions (coordinated mental states)—that come apart in their behavior but are falsely unified by theorists because they co-occur in paradigm cases.
sketch: The argument proceeds by showing that the two mechanisms have different persistence conditions, different update rules, and different effects on downstream speech acts. Conversational score persists through the interaction and constrains propriety of moves even when participants privately reject the content (as in legal proceedings), while shared suppositions are fragile mental coordinations that evaporate when mutual belief fails. The key premise is that what licenses presupposition and what licenses accommodation are distinct phenomena: presupposition draws on public score (hence why you can presuppose what you know your audience rejects in adversarial contexts), while accommodation requires actual mental coordination (hence why accommodation fails when mutual belief is missing). Paradigm cooperative conversations obscure this because both mechanisms align, but adversarial, institutional, and strategic discourse reveal their independence.
target: The shared assumption between Stalnaker and Yalcin that common ground is a unified phenomenon located either in iterated attitudes or knowledge-of-acceptance
risk: The two phenomena may be aspects of a single mechanism with context-sensitive weighting rather than truly distinct kinds, or the purported different behaviors may be explicable within a unified framework by adding complexity to the update rules
promise_reason: Two-mechanism proposal is plausible but needs stronger evidence that they genuinely come apart rather than being aspects of one thing.

thesis: Presupposition accommodation shows that common ground cannot be constituted by any combination of acceptances or beliefs, because accommodation updates common ground before any participant forms the corresponding attitude—the public commitment leads rather than follows mental state convergence.
sketch: Classic accommodation cases: 'I'm picking up my sister from the airport' presupposes the speaker has a sister; if this is news to you, you accommodate—the proposition enters common ground. But trace the temporal order: the moment of accommodation is the moment you recognize the presupposition and don't challenge it. At that very moment, do you believe the speaker has a sister? Not necessarily—you might be agnostic, or even suspicious. Do you accept it? You haven't decided yet; acceptance (in Yalcin's voluntary sense) requires uptake and endorsement you haven't completed. Yet the proposition is already in play—already common ground—because subsequent discourse treats it as such and you'll be the one at fault if you belatedly challenge it. The key premise is that common ground update is an affair of micro-seconds, completed on recognition of the presupposition trigger, while mental state formation (belief, acceptance, even knowledge-that-it's-accepted) takes longer and may never complete. Therefore common ground is not constituted by these mental states; at best they're usual effects of common ground being established.
target: Both views' constitutive claims about mental states and common ground, particularly Yalcin's knowledge-of-acceptance account
risk: Theorists may argue that the non-challenge itself constitutes a form of immediate, thin acceptance, or that there's an implicit acceptance in continuing the conversation that's fast enough to avoid the counterexample
promise_reason: Temporal priority argument is interesting but mentalists have responses about dispositional states; needs tighter empirical case.

thesis: The phenomenon of conversational repair reveals that common ground is not what the participants accept or believe but what they are committed to defending: common ground consists of propositions whose denial requires justification, even when all parties privately reject them.
sketch: Examine the pragmatics of repair and challenge: once a proposition has been asserted and not challenged, any participant who later wants to question it must perform repair work—'Wait, actually...' or 'I should have said earlier...' This repair requirement exists even when everyone knows nobody believes the proposition (as in certain bargaining scenarios: 'For purposes of this negotiation, we're assuming the property is worth $X' / later: 'Actually, we need to revisit that assumption'). The key premise is that what makes something common ground is not that parties have attitudes toward it, but that it occupies a default status requiring justificatory work to dislodge. Common ground is the set of propositions that are dialectically 'safe' unless challenged. This is a normative structure—about what moves require defense—not a mental structure. This explains why common ground can include things nobody believes (institutional contexts), things only some participants know (after failed accommodation), and things everyone has forgotten (lengthy proceedings). The mental states theorists point to are heuristics for what will require defense, not constitutive of that defensive requirement.
target: The shared assumption that common ground is a descriptive notion about mental states rather than a normative notion about dialectical burdens
risk: The normative reframing may be accused of changing the subject—explaining conversational obligations rather than conversational context—or the normative facts may be argued to supervene on mental states after all (we're committed to defending what we've accepted)
promise_reason: Repair phenomena support publicist views but this framing as 'requiring justification' is already implicit in commitment accounts.

thesis: Treating common ground as a mental state commits you to denying that groups can be mistaken about what their own common ground contains, but we attribute such mistakes routinely.
sketch: If common ground is constituted by participants' attitudes (whether iterated belief, acceptance, or knowledge-of-acceptance), then the participants have collective first-person authority about what's in common ground—it contains exactly what their attitudes make it contain. But we regularly say things like 'the committee thought they'd established that p, but actually it was never in common ground because Jones's earlier statement was misunderstood by everyone.' This isn't a claim about what they believed about their beliefs; it's a claim that the common ground had different contents than all participants took it to have. The key premise is that mental-state constitution makes such third-person corrections incoherent: there's no gap between the mental facts and what they constitute. If common ground is a structure of public commitments, however, it can outrun participants' grasp of it, just as legal obligations can.
target: Both Stalnaker's and Yalcin's mentalist frameworks
risk: Mentalists can reply that apparent 'mistakes about common ground' are really mistakes about what attitudes participants held—Jones didn't actually accept p even though others thought she did—preserving mental-state constitution.
promise_reason: Group-mistake cases are good evidence but mentalists can appeal to collective misrepresentation; needs more to be decisive.

thesis: Common ground is neither mental states nor public commitments but the set of propositions that would survive idealized mutual recognition of the discourse's actual history.
sketch: Both mentalists and publicists assume common ground is constituted by some actual feature of the situation—either participant attitudes or observable commitments. But conversational practice treats common ground as essentially counterfactual: what matters is what would be mutually recognized as shared if all participants were ideally attentive to what's actually happened in the discourse. The key premise is that our ordinary practices of disputing and correcting common ground claims ('that wasn't established—you didn't hear her qualifier') presuppose a normative standard independent of both actual attitudes and actual public records.
